final_answer:
No. Under Texas law the trial court did not err (and did not abuse its discretion) in disqualifying Smith Fullingham. This fact pattern tracks In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026) (orig. proceeding), where the Supreme Court of Texas denied mandamus relief against a disqualification order.

Framework (Texas Supreme Court, controlling): Disqualification is a severe remedy, and the movant must show actual prejudice; but for nonlawyer assistants who switch sides, Texas applies a two-step test with different presumptions at each step (Phoenix Founders v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994); In re American Home Products, 985 S.W.2d 68 (Tex. 1998); In re Columbia Valley Healthcare, 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010); In re Turner, 542 S.W.3d 553 (Tex. 2017)).

Step 1 - did the nonlawyer acquire confidences? If the nonlawyer actually worked on the same matter for the former firm, the law irrebuttably presumes she obtained confidential information, so the movant need not reveal the confidences. Jones prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications and attended strategy meetings on the Apex-Prestige suit, so step 1 is satisfied. The 2011 withdrawal of Owens Farmer, her 2013 departure, and her claimed lack of recall do not matter; the presumption is irrebuttable.

Step 2 - did she share them with the new firm? Here the presumption is rebuttable, but only by showing the new firm took the required prophylactic measures: the firm must instruct the nonlawyer, at or before the time she begins work on the conflicted matter, not to work on any matter on which she worked at the prior employer, and to not disclose confidences, and must take reasonable steps to enforce that instruction (Turner; Columbia Valley; American Home Products). If those measures were not taken, the presumption of sharing becomes irrebuttable and disqualification of the firm is mandatory. Zaidi reaffirmed this even where the conflict emerged years after hiring (the firm there hired the assistant before it took on the case): the firm must give the instruction when the conflict arises or the assistant is first assigned to the matter. Smith Fullingham did not even ask about her prior work, did nothing in 2017, and Jones worked on the matter thirteen times and e-filed two documents in her name. The screen announced only in January 2023 came years too late; late screening cannot cure the conflict. Her assertion that she shared nothing and does not recall her work is irrelevant because the firm may not rebut with testimony that no confidences were shared, and the limited, secretarial nature of her tasks does not change the result (Zaidi applied the rule to a legal assistant doing a few case-related secretarial tasks).

Waiver: Disqualification can be waived by unreasonable delay after the movant learns of the conflict (In re EPIC Holdings, 985 S.W.2d 41 (Tex. 1998); Vaughan v. Walther, 875 S.W.2d 690 (Tex. 1994)). Delay is judged from actual knowledge, and the party asserting waiver bears the burden. Apex learned of Jones in January 2023 via a filing notification; the firm's response stated she would be screened; Apex moved in early March 2023, about two months later. Zaidi held that e-filing notifications listing the assistant's name do not as a matter of law establish actual knowledge from 2022, and that a roughly two-month interval spent investigating before moving was not waiver as a matter of law. The earlier March 2022 filing notices therefore do not show waiver, and a two-month delay is not unreasonable. At minimum, the trial court's refusal to find waiver was within its discretion.

Conclusion: Because (1) Jones actually worked on the same matter, (2) the firm gave no timely instruction or screen, and (3) waiver was not established, disqualification of the entire firm was required. The trial court did not err. Caveat: I could not retrieve the full text of Zaidi or Turner (the sites were blocked), so details come from search-result summaries and case-law memory; the exact standard for the content of the required instruction and the Zaidi quotations should be verified against the opinion. Also, the Texas Disciplinary Rules (Rule 5.03) and the lack of any Texas rule permitting screening of nonlawyers who worked on the same matter after the fact do not change the result.

Whether the hiring firm can rebut the presumption of sharing with a screen or admonition adopted only after years of work and after the movant's inquiry

authorities.title: In re Adeel Zaidi, A.K. Chagla and Prestige Consulting d/b/a Turnaround Management Group
authorities.proposition: Firm must instruct side-switching nonlawyer at or before she begins work on conflicted matter not to work on it, even if conflict arises years after hire; late screening insufficient; e-filing notices do not establish waiver as a matter of law; mandamus denied.

authorities.title: In re Turner
authorities.proposition: Two-step test: irrebuttable presumption that nonlawyer who worked on same matter acquired confidences; presumption of sharing rebuttable only through required prophylactic measures; otherwise disqualification mandatory.

authorities.citation: Phoenix Founders, Inc. v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994)
authorities.title: Phoenix Founders v. Marshall
authorities.proposition: Paralegal conflicts; presumption of acquired confidences; screening may rebut sharing presumption.

authorities.proposition: Nonlawyer who worked on same matter: firm disqualified absent proper screening; irrebuttable presumption of acquired confidences.

claims.text: The trial court did not err; disqualification of Smith Fullingham was required.
Jones's work on the same matter at Owens Farmer creates an irrebuttable presumption she acquired confidences.
Absent a timely instruction/screen when she began work on the matter, the sharing presumption is irrebuttable; the January 2023 screen came too late.
Apex did not waive: e-filing notices do not establish knowledge as a matter of law and about two months to investigate and move was not unreasonable delay.
